{{Cheatsheet}}

Docker packages software into lightweight, isolated containers, each run from a read-only image.

New to Docker? [https://docs.docker.com/get-started/ Get Started] runs your first container

== Basic example: serve a website ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" line highlight="2,4" copy>
docker pull nginx                       # fetch the image
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx  # start a container from it
docker ps                               # is it running?
curl localhost:8080                     # yes — the nginx welcome page
docker stop web && docker rm web        # stop and remove it
</syntaxhighlight>

An '''image''' is a read-only template; a '''container''' is one running instance of it. Containers are throwaway — anything written inside them vanishes when the container is removed, unless kept in a [[#Volumes|volume]].

== Running containers ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
docker run -it ubuntu bash              # interactive terminal
docker run -d --name db postgres:16     # detached, named
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx             # host 8080 → container 80
docker run -v ./data:/app/data app      # mount a host directory
docker run --rm -it app                 # remove the container on exit
docker run -e MODE=prod app             # set an environment variable
</syntaxhighlight>

{| class="wikitable"
! Flag !! Effect
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-d</syntaxhighlight> || run detached (in the background)
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-it</syntaxhighlight> || interactive terminal (needed for bash)
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-p host:container</syntaxhighlight> || publish a port
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-v host:container</syntaxhighlight> || mount a volume or directory
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>--name</syntaxhighlight> || give the container a name
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>--rm</syntaxhighlight> || auto-remove once it stops
|-
| <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-e KEY=value</syntaxhighlight> || set an environment variable
|}

<blockquote>
'''Port order is always host:container''' — <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-p 8080:80</syntaxhighlight> means your machine's 8080 forwards to the container's 80, not the other way round.
</blockquote>

== Managing containers ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
docker ps                    # running containers
docker ps -a                 # all, including stopped
docker logs -f web           # follow the logs
docker exec -it web bash     # shell inside a running container
docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf .   # copy a file out of a container
docker stop web              # stop one
docker start web             # start an existing (stopped) one
docker rm web                # remove a stopped container
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker run</syntaxhighlight> always creates a new container.''' Re-run the same task? <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker stop</syntaxhighlight> / <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker start</syntaxhighlight> the existing one instead — or use [[#Docker Compose|Compose]].
</blockquote>

== Images ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
docker build -t myapp .           # build an image from the Dockerfile
docker images                     # list local images
docker pull postgres:16           # fetch an image (or a tag)
docker push user/myapp:v1         # upload to a registry
docker tag myapp user/myapp:v1    # retag
docker rmi myapp                  # remove an image
</syntaxhighlight>

== Dockerfile ==

A plain text recipe that <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker build</syntaxhighlight> turns into an image:

<syntaxhighlight lang="dockerfile" copy>
FROM python:3.12-slim     # base image
WORKDIR /app              # working directory for the rest
COPY requirements.txt .   # copy file(s) into the image
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .                  # everything else
CMD ["python", "app.py"]  # default command when run
</syntaxhighlight>

== Volumes ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy">
docker run -v ./data:/app/data app     # bind mount: a host directory
docker run -v data-vol:/data app       # named volume, managed by Docker
docker volume ls                       # list named volumes
docker volume prune                    # remove unused ones
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''Without a volume, container data is lost on <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker rm</syntaxhighlight>.''' The database keeps its data only because something like <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>-v db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data</syntaxhighlight> is mounted.
</blockquote>

== Docker Compose ==

Multi-container setups described in YAML — start, stop and rebuild everything with one command:

<syntaxhighlight lang="yaml" copy>
services:
  web:
    build: .                    # build from the Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data
  db:
    image: postgres:16          # or pull a ready-made image
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
</syntaxhighlight>

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
docker compose up -d          # start everything in the background
docker compose up --build     # rebuild images, then start
docker compose ps             # status of all services
docker compose logs -f        # follow the combined logs
docker compose down           # stop and remove the containers
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''The modern command is <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker compose</syntaxhighlight> (space).''' The old v1 tool was a separate binary spelled <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker-compose</syntaxhighlight> (hyphen) — you may still see it in older tutorials.
</blockquote>

== Cleanup ==

<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" copy>
docker system prune      # dangling images, stopped containers, unused networks and cache
docker system prune -a   # ... plus every image no container uses
docker system df         # disk usage by images, containers, volumes
</syntaxhighlight>

<blockquote>
'''<syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker system prune -a</syntaxhighlight> removes images you are not running.''' Images you might want again later need a <syntaxhighlight lang="bash" inline>docker pull</syntaxhighlight> — they are not lost, just re-fetched.
</blockquote>
